advice.CHARGE: Compare generation and eclipse energy separately; Sun pointing and fewer powered loads help recharge.
advice.DOWNLINK: Observe, then send during contact. A faster radio needs extra electricity and may need Earth pointing.
advice.FUEL: Compare a wider capture path, lighter dry hardware or a more efficient engine, then plan fuel again.
advice.OBSERVE: Switch the mission instrument on, meet its pointing and sunlight needs, and allow time to return its data.
advice.PROTECT: Turn off unneeded instruments or enter SAFE during elevated dose. SAFE does not shield radiation; leave SAFE explicitly afterward.

assumption.hardware: Hardware specifications are authored game abstractions, not qualified manufacturer specifications.
assumption.model.agingDayFraction: Aging event at 60% of mission duration, with seeded ±10 percentage points.
assumption.model.batteryAgingFraction: Scheduled capacity loss is 10%, an engineering-game event, not a fitted aging law.
assumption.model.batteryLowPct: Auto-pause on downward crossing of 20% remaining charge.
assumption.model.brownoutFatalHours: A continuous depleted-battery interval of twelve hours is fatal.
assumption.model.captureMargin: Fuel planning includes 10% capture delta-v margin; the arrival burn uses its exact computed requirement.
assumption.model.coarseScience: Coarse magnetic pointing halves target-instrument data production.
assumption.model.cueCooldownSec: Minimum time between separate raises of a coaching cue.
assumption.model.daySec: Operational durations use Earth days of 86,400 seconds; Mars operational objective time begins after capture, separate from cruise.
assumption.model.dsnHours: Mars antenna allocation per Earth day; geometry also tests planetary occultation.
assumption.model.forecastStepSec: One-day forecast sampling interval in seconds.
assumption.model.healthThreshold: Healthy time requires battery at least 20% charged and no current fatal condition.
assumption.model.historyEverySec: Telemetry history sampling interval in simulated seconds.
assumption.model.marsBackground: Assumed Mars-orbit background µGy/h; no calibrated orbital dataset is claimed.
assumption.model.sunBackground: Assumed interplanetary background µGy/h for a Sun-centred craft, the order of cruise-phase dosimeter readings; held constant with distance from the Sun, and no calibrated dataset is claimed.
assumption.model.marsStormDay: Mars storm begins ten operational days after capture; historical CME is narrative context only.
assumption.model.marsStormDose: Assumed orbital µGy/h during the Mars storm; the NASA Curiosity surface total is not used as an orbital rate.
assumption.model.maxFrameSteps: Per-call fixed-step work cap; oversized requests emit WARP_LIMITED.
assumption.model.minElevation: Station contact minimum elevation in degrees.
assumption.model.monitorRiskFactor: Radiation monitors are more tolerant in the assumed powered-electronics risk model, not physically shielded by SAFE.
assumption.model.outageHours: One scripted six-hour ground outage for Earth missions.
assumption.model.pointingEarth: EARTH solar generation fraction relative to SUN.
assumption.model.pointingSun: Mode-based attitude model, not a rigid-body attitude simulation.
assumption.model.pointingTarget: TARGET solar generation fraction relative to SUN.
assumption.model.propellantCostPerKg: Budget-unit cost per kg of propellant, charged in addition to dry engine hardware.
assumption.model.radiationReplay: The ISS hourly record is replayed at the chosen Earth orbit as an environment approximation. Co-occurrence with a DONKI storm does not attribute each reading to that storm. SAFE changes powered electronics, not dose or shielding.
assumption.model.rides: Fixed rides offer 420 km/51.6°, 500 km/45°, 550 km/97°. A custom launcher offers circular Earth 350–800 km, inclination 0–98°. Mars capture offers 400 km periapsis, apoapsis 400/5000/10000/33000 km, zero inclination. The ride supplies departure delta-v. These are game choices, not actual launch offers.
assumption.model.scoreMargins: Time without modeled operational margin warnings score weight.
assumption.model.scoreTeam: Role sign-off and design-review collaboration score weight.
assumption.model.smallLauncherCost: SmallSat custom launcher price in abstract budget units (CubeSat price is 60).
assumption.model.stationLat: Single mid-latitude station latitude in degrees north.
assumption.model.stationLon: Single station longitude in degrees east.
assumption.model.storageWarningPct: Auto-pause on upward crossing of 90% storage occupancy.
assumption.model.sunDuty: Forecast plan: 60% SUN, 30% TARGET, 10% EARTH. Actual commands, not this forecast, fly the mission.
assumption.model.twoBody: No J2, drag, third-body perturbations, thermal model, axial tilt or penumbra. Earth and Mars use circular coplanar heliocentric paths at an optimal Hohmann window.
assumption.model.upsetK: Exponential electronics loss hazard per excess µGy/h per powered hour; independent of shielding. Radiation monitor sensitivity is scaled separately.
assumption.model.upsetThreshold: Gameplay upset threshold in µGy/h; not inferred from the ISS dose record.
assumption.model.usableDepth: Battery usable planning depth; simulation tracks the full physical capacity.
assumption.orbits: Ideal two-body paths omit drag, J2 and third-body perturbations.

glossary.battery-storage.def: A battery keeps a limited store of energy for times when generation cannot cover the load.
glossary.capture-burn.def: A capture burn slows the arriving spacecraft so Mars can keep it in a bound orbit.
glossary.capture-burn.term: Slowing down to stay at Mars
glossary.command-delay.def: A queued command is a request still traveling; it is not yet a spacecraft action.
glossary.concept-maturity.def: Concept maturity describes how much evidence supports a mission idea, not how exciting it sounds.
glossary.coverage.def: Coverage describes which places or opportunities a spacecraft can reach from its path.
glossary.cubesat-size.def: A CubeSat uses standardized packaging units so it can fit a compatible launch dispenser.
glossary.data-return.def: A measurement helps a sent-home objective only after its data is received on Earth.
glossary.data-storage.def: Storage holds measurements until the spacecraft can send them home.
glossary.eclipse.def: A planetary eclipse is a part of the path where the planet blocks sunlight from the spacecraft.
glossary.energy-budget.def: Panels make electricity; equipment uses it; batteries store some for later.
glossary.game-budget.def: Budget units let you compare choices without pretending to quote real mission prices.
glossary.ground-contact.def: The spacecraft can communicate only when the model gives it a usable path to the ground station.
glossary.inclination.def: Inclination describes how much an orbit is tilted relative to the planet’s equator.
glossary.instrument-risk.def: Radiation can disrupt electronics, but a dose reading alone does not tell us an instrument’s exact failure chance.
glossary.kepler-orbits.def: The game follows ideal paths determined by gravity between a spacecraft and one main body.
glossary.launch-rides.def: A launch ride delivers a compatible spacecraft to an allowed starting path.
glossary.light-time.def: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, not instantly.
glossary.light-time.term: Time for a signal to travel
glossary.mass-volume.def: A spacecraft must fit both a mass limit and a separate space limit.
glossary.mission-design.def: Designing a mission means choosing hardware and operations that can meet a goal together.
glossary.mission-failure.def: A failure report connects a recorded condition with the choices that could change the next attempt.
glossary.mission-goal.def: A mission goal says what useful result the spacecraft must achieve.
glossary.model-assumptions.def: An assumption is a stated simplification or invented game setting, not a measured fact.
glossary.orbit-height.def: Altitude is the spacecraft’s distance above the model planet’s reference surface.
glossary.orbit-shape.def: An oval orbit comes closer to the planet at one end and travels farther away at the other.
glossary.orbital-period.def: Orbital period is the time needed to complete one trip around the planet.
glossary.pointing.def: Pointing chooses which direction the spacecraft and its instruments face.
glossary.propulsion.def: A rocket changes spacecraft motion by pushing exhaust in the opposite direction.
glossary.radiation.def: Absorbed dose describes energy deposited by radiation in matter; dose rate describes how fast that happens.
glossary.radio-links.def: A radio sends information using electromagnetic signals, with limited speed and electricity.
glossary.rocket-equation.def: More propellant allows more speed change, but the spacecraft must accelerate that propellant before it is used.
glossary.safe-mode.def: Safe mode changes how the spacecraft operates; it does not block radiation.
glossary.safety-margins.def: A safety margin leaves some capacity unused so small changes do not immediately break the plan.
glossary.science-return.def: Science return describes the useful results achieved for the mission’s stated goal.
glossary.smallsat-class.def: A SmallSat is a small-spacecraft class, not a promise that every mission will fit.
glossary.solar-distance.def: Farther from the Sun, the same panel receives less sunlight.
glossary.source-evidence.def: Evidence tells you who produced a value, what was measured, and where its use may be limited.
glossary.specific-impulse.def: Specific impulse compares how much push an engine gets from a given flow of propellant.
glossary.systems-tradeoffs.def: A change that helps one system can make another system work harder.
glossary.transfer-orbits.def: A transfer orbit carries the spacecraft around the Sun from Earth’s neighborhood toward Mars.

science.battery-storage.consequence: A bigger battery can last longer but adds mass, room and cost. Reducing demand helps but can reduce observations or return.
science.battery-storage.context: The design forecast reserves part of rated capacity for uncertainty; flight tracks the full physical charge. Shadow and transmitting can drain it.
science.battery-storage.deeper: Capacity is energy in Wh, not power in W. State of charge compares remaining Wh with physical capacity. The design forecast uses its disclosed usable fraction as a planning reserve. At constant load, hours of endurance equal available Wh divided by unmet load in W.
science.battery-storage.diagram: A tank-shaped energy store fills from panel surplus and drains when equipment demand exceeds generation.
science.battery-storage.limitations: Usable depth, battery aging and the depletion-failure timer are assumptions. Real batteries depend on temperature, current, chemistry and cycle history.
science.battery-storage.summary: A battery keeps a limited store of energy for times when generation cannot cover the load.
science.battery-storage.title: Battery energy storage
science.capture-burn.consequence: Compare a wider path, lighter hardware or engine efficiency, then confirm enough fuel including the disclosed planning margin.
science.capture-burn.context: A close circular capture usually needs more slowing than a wide oval option in this arrival model. Feasibility depends on your actual design.
science.capture-burn.deeper: At the close point, the model compares hyperbolic arrival speed with the selected bound-orbit speed. Their difference is required capture Δv in km/s. Fuel use follows the rocket equation; radii are measured from Mars’s center.
science.capture-burn.diagram: Incoming open path → braking arrow at the close point → closed Mars ellipse; insufficient braking leaves the path open.
science.capture-burn.limitations: Instantaneous braking, ideal arrival geometry and no aerobraking are assumed. No fixed Δv value universally proves that the entire SmallSat class is infeasible.
science.capture-burn.summary: A capture burn slows the arriving spacecraft so Mars can keep it in a bound orbit.
science.capture-burn.title: Slowing down to stay at Mars
science.command-delay.consequence: Review the queue and current spacecraft state before sending more. Opposite requests do not instantly cancel earlier ones.
science.command-delay.context: Mars commands have delivery timestamps. Conditions can change before receipt, and a request can be refused when it arrives.
science.command-delay.deeper: For ordinary Mars commands, delivery time equals issue time plus modeled one-way light time. Pending, delivered, refused and actively transmitting are different states. Capture confirmation is a pre-arranged arrival action.
science.command-delay.diagram: Timeline: issue command → pending interval → receive and validate → delivered action or refusal; a later command has its own timeline.
science.command-delay.limitations: The queue is an educational command model, not an operational flight software protocol. Reading help freezes simulation timestamps without changing queued requests.
science.command-delay.summary: A queued command is a request still traveling; it is not yet a spacecraft action.
science.command-delay.title: Pending and delivered commands
science.concept-maturity.consequence: Check requirements and trade-offs before committing; more detail can reveal costs as well as opportunities.
science.concept-maturity.context: Professional design notes use concept maturity levels to describe growing knowledge about a proposed mission.
science.concept-maturity.deeper: Concept Maturity Levels, abbreviated CML, organize the development of mission concepts. They are not flight-hardware Technology Readiness Levels and do not certify a spacecraft.
science.concept-maturity.diagram: Early idea → compared options → checked requirements → supported design; evidence grows at each step.
science.concept-maturity.limitations: The game stages are an educational mapping, not an official CML assessment.
science.concept-maturity.summary: Concept maturity describes how much evidence supports a mission idea, not how exciting it sounds.
science.concept-maturity.title: How developed is the idea?
science.coverage.consequence: Choose a path that supports your goal and station access; compare forecast data return as well as geometry.
science.coverage.context: Inclination, height, planet rotation, sunlight and pointing affect opportunities differently. A larger visible area is not automatically more useful science.
science.coverage.deeper: A ground track is the moving point beneath a spacecraft on a rotating planet. Contact is a station-visibility condition; observation also needs the instrument’s mode and lighting conditions.
science.coverage.diagram: Tilted orbit above a rotating planet traces a ground path; only some segments line up with a target, sunlight and a ground station.
science.coverage.limitations: The game does not produce a validated revisit map, sensor footprint, image-resolution model or global mission-coverage assessment.
science.coverage.summary: Coverage describes which places or opportunities a spacecraft can reach from its path.
science.coverage.title: Where observations and contacts happen
science.cubesat-size.consequence: Smaller parts leave room for other hardware but may offer less energy, storage or accuracy.
science.cubesat-size.context: This mission uses a 3U class: room is limited to 3 U and mass must be below the cited 4 kg class limit.
science.cubesat-size.deeper: U is a CubeSat packaging unit based on a roughly 10 cm-sided unit. Three units form the nominal 3U format; the full mechanical specification includes rails, clearances and tolerances.
science.cubesat-size.diagram: Three connected unit boxes form a 3U envelope; equipment and structure must fit the permitted mass and packaging.
science.cubesat-size.limitations: The game applies its cited CubeSat 101 class rule, not every current dispenser specification. Actual launch requirements must be checked for each provider.
science.cubesat-size.summary: A CubeSat uses standardized packaging units so it can fit a compatible launch dispenser.
science.cubesat-size.title: CubeSat size
science.data-return.consequence: Send during contact or compare radios. Faster sending needs electricity and may need Earth pointing.
science.data-return.context: Turning on the camera fills onboard storage; it does not automatically increase returned data.
science.data-return.deeper: Data volume is measured in bytes: this model uses decimal MB = 1,000,000 bytes. Radio rates use kbps = 1,000 bits per second; 8 bits make one byte. Return is limited by stored data, contact, mode and link rate.
science.data-return.diagram: Instrument → onboard storage → radio during contact → Earth; only the last arrow increases returned-data progress.
science.data-return.limitations: Compression, packet loss, coding and detailed ground processing are not modeled. Generated and returned volumes are separate counters.
science.data-return.summary: A measurement helps a sent-home objective only after its data is received on Earth.
science.data-return.title: Data sent home
science.data-storage.consequence: Add storage for a larger buffer or send more often. More storage does not itself improve the link or meet the objective.
science.data-storage.context: If instruments generate data faster than the radio returns it, the buffer fills and new data may be lost.
science.data-storage.deeper: Stored MB changes by generated MB minus transmitted MB, bounded between zero and capacity. Buffer fullness is stored volume divided by capacity, shown as a percentage.
science.data-storage.diagram: Measurements fill a finite box; downlink empties it; overflow cannot be stored.
science.data-storage.limitations: Storage capacities and instrument rates are assumptions. The game does not model file priorities, compression or physical memory wear.
science.data-storage.summary: Storage holds measurements until the spacecraft can send them home.
science.data-storage.title: Onboard storage
science.eclipse.consequence: Store more usable energy or reduce shadow-time demand; each choice costs hardware resources or observing time.
science.eclipse.context: Panels stop generating in shadow, so the battery must cover equipment that stays on.
science.eclipse.deeper: The model treats the planet’s shadow as a cylinder opposite the Sun. Eclipse fraction is time in that shadow divided by orbital period. Required shadow energy depends on load in W and shadow duration in hours.
science.eclipse.diagram: Sun → planet → cylindrical shadow; the spacecraft path crosses sunlight and shadow, with the battery supplying the dark segment.
science.eclipse.limitations: No penumbra, atmospheric refraction or seasonal solar-plane model is included. A forecast average does not describe every real pass.
science.eclipse.summary: A planetary eclipse is a part of the path where the planet blocks sunlight from the spacecraft.
science.eclipse.title: Planetary shadow
science.energy-budget.consequence: Larger panels improve generation but add mass and cost. Switching equipment off saves energy but pauses its work.
science.energy-budget.context: Check average generation and shadow survival separately. A daily surplus does not guarantee enough stored energy for an eclipse.
science.energy-budget.deeper: Power P, in watts (W), is an energy-transfer rate. Energy E, in watt-hours (Wh), equals constant power P multiplied by duration t in hours: E = P × t. The core integrates changing generation and load.
science.energy-budget.diagram: Sunlight → panels → equipment; surplus → battery; during shadow the battery → equipment.
science.energy-budget.limitations: Panel ratings, loads, pointing factors and forecast operating fractions are game assumptions. No thermal or detailed electrical model is simulated.
science.energy-budget.summary: Panels make electricity; equipment uses it; batteries store some for later.
science.energy-budget.title: Making and using electricity
science.game-budget.consequence: A cheaper choice leaves room for another capability, but may limit power, communication or science.
science.game-budget.context: Every starting part, upgrade and ride uses the same visible mission budget.
science.game-budget.deeper: Budget units are an authored game resource. They are not dollars, procurement estimates, exchange rates or financial predictions. Difficulty can change the available game budget.
science.game-budget.diagram: Available budget splits into structure, equipment, launch and fuel planning; unused units remain available.
science.game-budget.limitations: Real mission costs include labor, testing, risk, operations and many other items not priced here.
science.game-budget.summary: Budget units let you compare choices without pretending to quote real mission prices.
science.game-budget.title: Game budget
science.ground-contact.consequence: Use available passes, but budget transmit electricity and pointing time; a radio request is not proof that sending is active.
science.ground-contact.context: An Earth pass is limited by the horizon and station elevation rule. Mars uses assumed antenna availability and modeled planetary blocking.
science.ground-contact.deeper: Elevation is the angle above the station’s local horizon, in degrees. Contact requires the modeled elevation threshold and no outage; Mars availability is a separate game scheduling assumption.
science.ground-contact.diagram: Planet with a station on its surface; a line to the satellite is usable only above the minimum elevation and without the planet blocking it.
science.ground-contact.limitations: One simplified station and availability pattern are not a global antenna network. Weather, link acquisition and real scheduling are omitted.
science.ground-contact.summary: The spacecraft can communicate only when the model gives it a usable path to the ground station.
science.ground-contact.title: Ground contact
science.inclination.consequence: Compare compatible launch paths; changing tilt is not a free post-launch maneuver in this game.
science.inclination.context: The tilt changes which latitudes the path can pass over and how it lines up with the ground station.
science.inclination.deeper: Inclination i is measured in degrees between the orbital plane and equatorial plane. Near 0° is equatorial; near 90° is polar; over 90° is retrograde.
science.inclination.diagram: Planetary equator as one plane and tilted orbit as another; the angle between them is inclination i.
science.inclination.limitations: A 97° path is not labeled sun-synchronous: the model does not simulate the precession needed to maintain that behavior.
science.inclination.summary: Inclination describes how much an orbit is tilted relative to the planet’s equator.
science.inclination.title: Orbit tilt
science.instrument-risk.consequence: Switch off unnecessary instruments to reduce modeled risk, at the cost of observations; protection is not guaranteed.
science.instrument-risk.context: The game adds a seeded, assumed risk for powered instruments during elevated radiation. Losing a required instrument can end the objective.
science.instrument-risk.deeper: A dose-rate-dependent hazard is converted into a probability over a time interval. Its coefficients and thresholds are game assumptions, not a fit to ISS DosTel1 failure measurements. The seed makes a command history reproducible.
science.instrument-risk.diagram: Measured environment → explicitly assumed risk rule → seeded outcome for an active instrument; no arrow claims the dose record measured a hardware failure.
science.instrument-risk.limitations: Electronics response depends on particle species, energy, device technology and shielding, which this model does not resolve. No universal failure probability can be inferred from the dose chart.
science.instrument-risk.summary: Radiation can disrupt electronics, but a dose reading alone does not tell us an instrument’s exact failure chance.
science.instrument-risk.title: Instrument risk
science.kepler-orbits.consequence: Change the chosen path and compare its consequences; opening equations does not change the physics or score.
science.kepler-orbits.context: Earth and Mars orbits are calculated from the same two-body rules in both Guided and Technical views.
science.kepler-orbits.deeper: Kepler propagation advances an elliptical orbit in time. The vis-viva relation is v² = μ(2/r − 1/a), with speed v in km/s, gravitational parameter μ in km³/s², orbital radius r and semimajor axis a in km.
science.kepler-orbits.diagram: Ellipse around one focus occupied by the planet; the spacecraft moves faster near periapsis and slower near apoapsis.
science.kepler-orbits.limitations: No drag, J2 precession, third-body perturbations or navigation uncertainty. Independent GMAT checks validate selected reference calculations, not a flight-certified trajectory.
science.kepler-orbits.summary: The game follows ideal paths determined by gravity between a spacecraft and one main body.
science.kepler-orbits.title: The orbit model
science.launch-rides.consequence: Changing rides can open a different path but spends game budget; compare compatibility before applying.
science.launch-rides.context: A dispenser offers fixed Earth paths; a dedicated ride allows the stated range. The Mars ride supplies departure, not capture fuel.
science.launch-rides.deeper: Altitude and inclination describe the delivered orbit. Departure speed change is provided by the Mars launch ride; slowing down at arrival belongs to the spacecraft.
science.launch-rides.diagram: Launch ride → allowed orbit choices → delivered spacecraft; Mars then requires a separate arrival burn.
science.launch-rides.limitations: Ride costs, availability and delivery choices are game assumptions, not commercial launch quotes or booking advice.
science.launch-rides.summary: A launch ride delivers a compatible spacecraft to an allowed starting path.
science.launch-rides.title: Launch rides
science.light-time.consequence: Plan ahead and distinguish sending a request from the spacecraft receiving it. Pausing to read help does not deliver queued commands.
science.light-time.context: Earth–Mars distance changes, so a command can take minutes to reach the spacecraft. The displayed delay comes from the current model.
science.light-time.deeper: One-way light time τ = d/c, where distance d is in km and c = 299792.458 km/s is the exact speed of light in vacuum. τ is in seconds. A reply needs another signal journey.
science.light-time.diagram: Earth sends a command → signal travels across distance d → Mars receives after τ; acknowledgment takes a separate return trip.
science.light-time.limitations: Planet positions use simplified circular paths, not a flight-navigation ephemeris. Processing delays and detailed communications protocols are omitted.
science.light-time.summary: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, not instantly.
science.light-time.title: Time for a signal to travel
science.mass-volume.consequence: Remove or replace hardware to save mass or room; check which capability you give up.
science.mass-volume.context: Structure, hardware and propellant all add mass. A light part can still use too much room.
science.mass-volume.deeper: Mass is measured in kilograms, kg; it is not the same as weight, a gravitational force. CubeSat packaging uses U; SmallSat room uses game bays. Launch mass limits are strict in this game.
science.mass-volume.diagram: Two separate bars: mass used / mass limit and room used / room limit. Passing one does not pass the other.
science.mass-volume.limitations: Packaging is a simplified sum of part volumes, not a three-dimensional fit or structural analysis. SmallSat bays are a game assumption.
science.mass-volume.summary: A spacecraft must fit both a mass limit and a separate space limit.
science.mass-volume.title: Mass and room
science.mission-design.consequence: Improve one system at a time and compare its effects on all budgets before confirming.
science.mission-design.context: The starting spacecraft is editable, and every included part uses mass, room and game budget.
science.mission-design.deeper: A mission moves from a need through concept, requirements, design, verification and operation. The game compresses these stages but keeps linked resource checks.
science.mission-design.diagram: Goal → spacecraft → hardware → launch path → operations → results, with redesign returning to hardware.
science.mission-design.limitations: The game does not replace engineering qualification, launch certification or a detailed mission study.
science.mission-design.summary: Designing a mission means choosing hardware and operations that can meet a goal together.
science.mission-design.title: Mission design
science.mission-failure.consequence: Use the recorded energy, data, instrument or fuel facts to redesign one cause at a time; compare the cost of each remedy.
science.mission-failure.context: The first failure keeps its own facts even if later events occur. A missed objective is different from a destroyed spacecraft.
science.mission-failure.deeper: Failure conditions include a sustained empty battery, loss of the last required instrument, failed capture or an unmet end-of-mission target. Difficulty sets disclosed recovery behavior; it does not change what an explanation costs.
science.mission-failure.diagram: Your design or command → recorded resource trend → first failure condition → specific alternative with a visible cost.
science.mission-failure.limitations: Failure timers and recovery penalties are game rules. A causal debrief describes this model’s recorded chain, not a forensic claim about real hardware.
science.mission-failure.summary: A failure report connects a recorded condition with the choices that could change the next attempt.
science.mission-failure.title: Understanding a mission setback
science.mission-goal.consequence: Choose an instrument that measures the right thing, then reserve electricity and a way to return its results.
science.mission-goal.context: Earth images and Mars maps count toward their goal only after data reaches Earth; Storm Watch counts valid storm-monitoring time.
science.mission-goal.deeper: Objectives are authored game requirements, not NASA mission specifications. MB means megabytes of data; h means hours. Progress compares the recorded objective metric with its required target.
science.mission-goal.diagram: Goal → measurement → stored data → returned result; storm monitoring also requires valid observing time.
science.mission-goal.limitations: Targets, mission lengths and scoring thresholds are game assumptions. A full progress bar is not a complete scientific validation.
science.mission-goal.summary: A mission goal says what useful result the spacecraft must achieve.
science.mission-goal.title: Mission goal
science.model-assumptions.consequence: Use forecasts to compare designs inside this model, and check limitations before applying a lesson to a real mission.
science.model-assumptions.context: Part ratings, costs, operating fractions, hazard rules and scoring are disclosed assumptions; sourced constants and archived readings have their own evidence.
science.model-assumptions.deeper: Calculated means a result derived from inputs and equations. Measured means an observation made by an instrument. Assumed means an authored input or rule. A calculation can contain both sourced and assumed inputs.
science.model-assumptions.diagram: Three labeled inputs—measured, sourced constant, assumed rule—feed a calculation; the output keeps the inputs’ limitations.
science.model-assumptions.limitations: The simulation omits thermal control, drag, J2 precession, detailed links and full mission qualification. Determinism does not make an assumption a physical law.
science.model-assumptions.summary: An assumption is a stated simplification or invented game setting, not a measured fact.
science.model-assumptions.title: What the model assumes
science.orbit-height.consequence: Compare paths for this spacecraft and goal. A different path can trade observing opportunities against communication or fuel.
science.orbit-height.context: Height changes period, shadow and contact geometry; use the computed preview rather than assuming higher is always better.
science.orbit-height.deeper: Orbital radius r equals planetary reference radius R plus altitude h; all three use km here. Gravity depends on distance from the center, not altitude alone.
science.orbit-height.diagram: Planet center → reference surface is R; surface → spacecraft is h; center → spacecraft is r = R + h.
science.orbit-height.limitations: The planet is idealized; terrain, atmospheric drag, orbital decay and detailed sensor resolution are not simulated.
science.orbit-height.summary: Altitude is the spacecraft’s distance above the model planet’s reference surface.
science.orbit-height.title: Orbit height
science.orbit-shape.consequence: A wider oval can need less arrival slowing, but is not universally better for contact, observing or power.
science.orbit-shape.context: Mars capture choices share a close point but have different far points, changing capture fuel, period and the operating geometry.
science.orbit-shape.deeper: Periapsis is closest approach and apoapsis is farthest. Semimajor axis a = (rₚ + rₐ)/2; eccentricity e = (rₐ − rₚ)/(rₐ + rₚ). Radii rₚ, rₐ and a are in km; e has no unit.
science.orbit-shape.diagram: Circle with equal near and far distances; ellipse with labeled periapsis near the planet and apoapsis farther away.
science.orbit-shape.limitations: Only ideal two-body ellipses are modeled; perturbations, orbit maintenance and detailed surface mapping quality are omitted.
science.orbit-shape.summary: An oval orbit comes closer to the planet at one end and travels farther away at the other.
science.orbit-shape.title: Circular and oval paths
science.orbital-period.consequence: Compare the computed period with battery and communication needs, not as a better-or-worse score by itself.
science.orbital-period.context: The period helps set the rhythm of shadow, observing and station passes; a pass is not guaranteed every orbit.
science.orbital-period.deeper: For a bound two-body orbit, T = 2π√(a³/μ). T is period in s, a is semimajor axis in km and μ is the planet’s gravitational parameter in km³/s². π is the circle constant, about 3.14159; √ means square root. The interface may convert seconds to minutes.
science.orbital-period.diagram: One loop around a planet marked start → halfway → start; elapsed time for the loop is T.
science.orbital-period.limitations: Two-body period ignores drag, oblateness, other bodies and active orbit changes.
science.orbital-period.summary: Orbital period is the time needed to complete one trip around the planet.
science.orbital-period.title: Time for one orbit
science.pointing.consequence: Choose a direction for the current task, accepting less generation or less observing time when the tasks compete.
science.pointing.context: Hold modes target Sun, target or Earth. Manual steering requests a quaternion attitude. Camera movement changes only the view.
science.pointing.deeper: Core tracks an attitude quaternion and slews toward its target at the installed ADCS rate. Body +X is the panel normal; +Z is the instrument and antenna boresight. Solar input uses panel-to-Sun geometry; science and directional links use their angular alignment.
science.pointing.diagram: One spacecraft with three labeled directions: Sun for charging, target for measuring, Earth for directional sending.
science.pointing.limitations: This is kinematic attitude slew, not integrated torque or rigid-body dynamics. Wheel momentum, saturation, flexible structures and orbit-changing thrust are not modeled.
science.pointing.summary: Pointing is the spacecraft orientation: panels, instrument and antenna must face useful directions.
science.pointing.title: Where the spacecraft points
science.propulsion.consequence: Compare engines and capture paths. Carrying more fuel adds mass and must fit both tank and spacecraft limits.
science.propulsion.context: Mars arrival requires your own engine and enough propellant to slow into the selected orbit.
science.propulsion.deeper: Delta-v, written Δv, measures a velocity change in km/s here. The available ideal Δv depends on engine exhaust performance and the ratio between fueled and unfueled mass.
science.propulsion.diagram: Exhaust arrow points backward; spacecraft velocity-change arrow points forward; braking reverses the thrust direction relative to travel.
science.propulsion.limitations: Burns are idealized impulses; finite burn time, guidance errors, tank pressure and engine reliability are not modeled.
science.propulsion.summary: A rocket changes spacecraft motion by pushing exhaust in the opposite direction.
science.propulsion.title: Changing spacecraft motion
science.radiation.consequence: Keep measuring for science or reduce powered-instrument exposure; safe mode stops observations but does not shield the spacecraft.
science.radiation.context: Storm Watch replays real ISS DosTel1 hourly means. The Mars storm’s orbital dose rate is separately assumed, not measured by the surface rover.
science.radiation.deeper: Absorbed dose uses gray, Gy = joule per kilogram. µGy/h means millionths of a gray each hour. Integrating dose rate over hours gives dose in µGy. Kp is a geomagnetic activity index, not dose; absorbed dose is not dose equivalent in sieverts.
science.radiation.diagram: Time axis →; measured dose-rate curve rises and falls. Area under that curve represents accumulated dose; source and location labels remain attached.
science.radiation.limitations: ISS Columbus measurements are local, not a calibrated map for every orbit. DONKI co-occurrence does not prove the cause of each peak. Curiosity’s reported 8100 µGy is a surface event total, not an orbital rate.
science.radiation.summary: Absorbed dose describes energy deposited by radiation in matter; dose rate describes how fast that happens.
science.radiation.title: Radiation measurements
science.radio-links.consequence: Compare useful data per contact with power use. A faster radio cannot send without stored data or a valid contact.
science.radio-links.context: The basic radio is slower but less demanding; a directional radio needs Earth pointing and sufficient transmit power.
science.radio-links.deeper: Rate is given in kbps, thousands of bits each second. Receive and transmit power are different W loads. The deep-space link rate uses the game’s inverse-square distance rule and a stated cap.
science.radio-links.diagram: Storage → powered transmitter → directed or broad radio beam → receiving station; contact and pointing gate the path.
science.radio-links.limitations: Rated rates, availability and distance scaling are game assumptions, not a complete link budget with noise, antenna gain and coding.
science.radio-links.summary: A radio sends information using electromagnetic signals, with limited speed and electricity.
science.radio-links.title: Radio communication
science.rocket-equation.consequence: Choose a wider arrival path, lighter hardware or a more efficient engine; each has a different cost.
science.rocket-equation.context: The fuel planner uses this design’s engine, dry mass and chosen capture requirement, then applies normal tank, mass and budget checks.
science.rocket-equation.deeper: Tsiolkovsky’s ideal equation is Δv = Isp × g₀ × ln(m₀/mf). Δv is in m/s, Isp in s, g₀ in m/s²; m₀ is fueled mass and mf is post-burn mass, both in kg. ln is the natural logarithm. The interface may show Δv in km/s.
science.rocket-equation.diagram: Dry spacecraft + propellant = initial mass m₀; after expelling propellant, remaining mass is mf; the mass ratio sets ideal Δv.
science.rocket-equation.limitations: An ideal single-stage impulse model omits unusable propellant, finite burns and guidance losses. A planning margin is an assumption, not a guarantee.
science.rocket-equation.summary: More propellant allows more speed change, but the spacecraft must accelerate that propellant before it is used.
science.rocket-equation.title: Fuel adds mass too
science.safe-mode.consequence: Use safe mode to prioritize operation under the assumed electronics-risk model, or keep only needed instruments on for science with remaining risk.
science.safe-mode.context: The game points toward the Sun, turns off instruments and leaves the radio receive-only. Storm measurements and downlink stop.
science.safe-mode.deeper: The relation between powered equipment, dose rate and failure probability is an explicit game assumption. Safe mode reduces exposure of powered instruments in that model, not the absorbed radiation field.
science.safe-mode.diagram: Radiation arrows still reach the spacecraft in safe mode; instrument switches are off and the solar panel faces the Sun.
science.safe-mode.limitations: No guarantee of survival and no physical shielding calculation. Real safe modes vary by spacecraft and do not establish the assumed probability rule.
science.safe-mode.summary: Safe mode changes how the spacecraft operates; it does not block radiation.
science.safe-mode.title: Safe mode is not shielding
science.safety-margins.consequence: Larger reserves can improve resilience but consume mass, space or budget that could support science.
science.safety-margins.context: The forecast checks mass, budget, electricity, battery and arrival fuel separately; one good margin cannot cancel a shortage elsewhere.
science.safety-margins.deeper: A margin compares available capacity with required use. Each displayed percentage follows the core’s stated denominator and threshold; the fuel planner uses a disclosed planning factor. A strict mass cap still applies at its exact boundary.
science.safety-margins.diagram: Capacity bar split into planned use and a labeled reserve; another resource can still be over its own limit.
science.safety-margins.limitations: Thresholds and planning factors are game assumptions, not certified reliability targets. No margin guarantees success against every omitted real-world effect.
science.safety-margins.summary: A safety margin leaves some capacity unused so small changes do not immediately break the plan.
science.safety-margins.title: Room for surprises
science.science-return.consequence: Balance observing with power, protection and communication. Review the result record rather than assuming more hardware means more science.
science.science-return.context: Image missions require returned MB; storm monitoring requires valid hours during the storm. Storage fullness is not success.
science.science-return.deeper: The objective component compares actual progress with its target and caps credit at completion. Other score components track game budget, health, margins and teamwork; weights are disclosed game assumptions.
science.science-return.diagram: Goal → valid observations → stored data → returned result; compare the relevant recorded metric with the target, not with storage fullness.
science.science-return.limitations: A game score is not scientific impact, publication quality or a real mission review. Photo counts are not invented from data volume.
science.science-return.summary: Science return describes the useful results achieved for the mission’s stated goal.
science.science-return.title: Useful science results
science.smallsat-class.consequence: A more efficient engine can reduce fuel needs but may cost more and use more room.
science.smallsat-class.context: Red Relay has more room than the CubeSat missions, but fuel and Mars hardware still compete under the mass cap.
science.smallsat-class.deeper: The cited NASA classification places SmallSats below 180 kg. This game gives the class 8 packaging bays as an explicit assumption; bays are not a NASA unit.
science.smallsat-class.diagram: Structure + hardware + propellant → total launch mass; separate equipment boxes occupy the game bays.
science.smallsat-class.limitations: Real small-spacecraft categories and interfaces vary. Feasibility depends on this design’s dry mass, engine, tank and arrival orbit.
science.smallsat-class.summary: A SmallSat is a small-spacecraft class, not a promise that every mission will fit.
science.smallsat-class.title: SmallSat class
science.solar-distance.consequence: Larger panels can compensate but add mass and cost; reducing demand sacrifices equipment use.
science.solar-distance.context: Mars receives less sunlight than Earth, so an Earth-rated panel does not deliver its full rated output there.
science.solar-distance.deeper: Solar irradiance S is power per area in W/m²: S = S₀(r₀/r)², where S₀ is irradiance at reference distance r₀; r and r₀ are distances from the Sun in km. NASA reference values are 1361.0 W/m² at Earth and 586.2 W/m² at Mars.
science.solar-distance.diagram: Two equal panels at different distances: sunlight spreads over a larger area at the farther panel, reducing received power per square meter.
science.solar-distance.limitations: The model uses representative orbital distances and idealized panel factors; degradation, temperature and dust are not detailed.
science.solar-distance.summary: Farther from the Sun, the same panel receives less sunlight.
science.solar-distance.title: Sunlight and distance
science.source-evidence.consequence: Open the source and compare its units, instrument, location and uncertainty with the claim before drawing a conclusion.
science.source-evidence.context: Source cards link archived measurements, constants and analyst records; snapshot retrieval time is different from observation time.
science.source-evidence.deeper: RadLab records keep instrument and UTC observation times; DONKI keeps event IDs and analyses. USGS facet counts describe a catalogue; product samples are title/name-matching heuristics because the export has no per-record mission field.
science.source-evidence.diagram: Source record → date, units and location checks → calculation or careful interpretation; assumptions are labeled separately.
science.source-evidence.limitations: Snapshots are not live feeds. An hourly mean is calculated from samples, not a new measurement. A matching product title is not verified mission attribution. A source link does not validate unrelated game assumptions.
science.source-evidence.summary: Evidence tells you who produced a value, what was measured, and where its use may be limited.
science.source-evidence.title: Where the numbers come from
science.specific-impulse.consequence: Compare the actual fuel preview for each engine rather than selecting by efficiency alone.
science.specific-impulse.context: A higher specific impulse can reduce the fuel needed for the same ideal speed change, but engine mass, cost and tank still matter.
science.specific-impulse.deeper: Specific impulse Isp is measured in seconds (s). Effective exhaust speed vₑ = Isp × g₀, where g₀ = 9.80665 m/s² is standard gravity and vₑ is in m/s. It is not the local gravity at Mars.
science.specific-impulse.diagram: Two engines perform the same velocity change; the higher-Isp engine can need a smaller propellant fraction, subject to its own mass and tank.
science.specific-impulse.limitations: Engine Isp ratings are game assumptions. The model does not vary performance with pressure, throttle or burn duration.
science.specific-impulse.summary: Specific impulse compares how much push an engine gets from a given flow of propellant.
science.specific-impulse.title: Engine efficiency: specific impulse
science.systems-tradeoffs.consequence: Compare gain and cost together, and review teammates’ sign-offs after changing the design.
science.systems-tradeoffs.context: A faster radio may return more data but draws more electricity; extra battery stores energy but adds mass and uses room.
science.systems-tradeoffs.deeper: A system budget tracks a separate resource such as kg of mass, W of power, Wh of stored energy or MB of data. Different units cannot be added into a single physical total.
science.systems-tradeoffs.diagram: Radio upgrade → faster return and higher electricity use → battery and panel review → mass and budget review.
science.systems-tradeoffs.limitations: Part specifications and operating schedules are simplified game assumptions. Forecasts are not automatic control.
science.systems-tradeoffs.summary: A change that helps one system can make another system work harder.
science.systems-tradeoffs.title: Connected choices
science.transfer-orbits.consequence: Plan the arrival orbit and fuel before skipping cruise. A convenient time jump does not supply missing propellant.
science.transfer-orbits.context: The launch ride supplies departure; the cruise summary advances the analytical trip but still stops for arrival and capture.
science.transfer-orbits.deeper: A Hohmann transfer is half an ideal ellipse tangent to two circular coplanar orbits. Transfer semimajor axis aₜ = (r₁ + r₂)/2; travel time t = π√(aₜ³/μ☉). r₁ and r₂ are Earth’s and Mars’s reference distances from the Sun in km; aₜ is in km, μ☉ is the Sun’s gravitational parameter in km³/s², and t is in s. π is the circle constant; √ means square root.
science.transfer-orbits.diagram: Sun at a focus; Earth and Mars circular reference paths joined by half of a transfer ellipse from departure to arrival.
science.transfer-orbits.limitations: Circular coplanar planetary paths, a met launch window and patched-conic transitions are assumed. No full ephemeris, midcourse corrections or gravity assists.
science.transfer-orbits.summary: A transfer orbit carries the spacecraft around the Sun from Earth’s neighborhood toward Mars.
science.transfer-orbits.title: Traveling from Earth to Mars

science.thermal-control.title: Thermal balance and heater
science.thermal-control.summary: The equipment bus gains and loses heat. Its heater trades battery energy for a usable temperature.
science.thermal-control.context: Technical missions model one bus temperature in kelvin. Sunlight, electrical loads and radiation to space change that temperature; a paid heater can be Off, On or Automatic.
science.thermal-control.consequence: Outside the operating range, science is inhibited. A sustained survival-limit violation can fail the mission. Reduce loads when hot; compare heater demand and battery reserve when cold.
science.thermal-control.deeper: The lumped balance is thermal capacity times temperature change equals absorbed external power plus internal heat and heater power minus radiative rejection. Flux must first be multiplied by effective area. Automatic control uses hysteresis to avoid rapid switching.
science.thermal-control.limitations: This is one authored thermal node, not a validated spacecraft thermal network. Coefficients and operating limits are exercise assumptions, not measured manufacturer data. See TECHNICAL_MODELS.md for units and omitted effects.
science.thermal-control.diagram: Sunlight and electrical loads heat the bus; radiation removes heat and the heater consumes stored electrical energy.
science.power-aging.title: Beginning- and end-of-life power
science.power-aging.summary: The array and battery gradually lose capability within a disclosed exercise envelope. A design must work at the end, not just launch.
science.power-aging.context: Technical launch checks use the same end-of-life factors as flight. Compare array output, usable battery capacity and the energy needed through eclipse.
science.power-aging.consequence: A small beginning-of-life surplus may become a deficit. Add charged hardware before launch or change duty, pointing and heater use in flight; no command repairs battery chemistry.
science.power-aging.deeper: A bounded monotonic factor scales array output and battery capacity over exercise time. If capacity falls below stored charge, excess charge is discarded rather than converted into new energy.
science.power-aging.limitations: Degradation is accelerated and authored for a short teaching exercise. It does not claim that a real array or battery loses this capability in a few days.
science.power-aging.diagram: Solar input charges a battery whose usable capacity and generation envelope decrease with exercise time.
science.pointing-recovery.title: Slew, settle and reacquire
science.pointing-recovery.summary: Requesting a direction is not the same as reaching it. Slewing and recovering degraded pointing take time and electrical energy.
science.pointing-recovery.context: Requested attitude, hold mode, rate and angular errors distinguish target from actual orientation. Camera mode never issues an attitude command.
science.pointing-recovery.consequence: Unsettled or degraded pointing reduces usable observation and directional communications. Reacquire pointing requests a bounded recovery; it does not repair damaged hardware.
science.pointing-recovery.deeper: Attitude follows a bounded ADCS angular rate; operational acquisition and seeded pointing degradation still apply. Reacquisition is an explicit command and retains normal transport and energy checks.
science.pointing-recovery.limitations: No torque integration, wheel momentum, saturation or magnetic desaturation is solved. Kinematic steering changes orientation, never the orbit.
science.pointing-recovery.diagram: A requested direction passes through acquisition before becoming settled; a degraded state requires explicit recovery.
science.link-resilience.title: Contact, allocation and robust links
science.link-resilience.summary: Seeing a station does not guarantee allocated service or a usable link. Robust mode trades throughput for tolerance of modeled degradation.
science.link-resilience.context: Technical telemetry distinguishes geometric contact, station allocation and effective quality. Uplink commands may wait for contact before propagation starts, then expire if their validity window passes.
science.link-resilience.consequence: Robust mode cannot send through a planet or an unavailable station. Read issue, transmission, arrival and result times separately; a requested command is not yet an applied action.
science.link-resilience.deeper: A reduced quality threshold and rate factor model resilience without inventing a decibel link margin. Arrival conditions are revalidated; a reboot can refuse a previously valid operational request.
science.link-resilience.limitations: Schedules and quality envelopes are authored, not live DSN service. Local readouts represent idealized onboard state; a separate telemetry-return-delay solver and full RF budget are not modeled.
science.link-resilience.diagram: A command waits for geometric contact and station allocation, travels at light speed, then receives a delivery or refusal result.
science.onboard-recovery.title: Onboard reset and deliberate recovery
science.onboard-recovery.summary: A computer reset stops science and transmission but keeps recorded data. Recovery costs time and energy, and finishes safely rather than restarting everything.
science.onboard-recovery.context: Technical scenarios include a seeded reset exercise with observable reboot state and cooldown. An independent low-rate recovery path is distinct from ordinary payload and pointing commands.
science.onboard-recovery.consequence: Wait for the recovery conditions, request recovery, then explicitly restore operations. Check queued requests: they retain timestamps and can be refused or expire rather than replaying silently.
science.onboard-recovery.deeper: Reset sheds loads without refilling the battery or erasing first-failure evidence. Ordinary requests received while rebooting are refused. Completed recovery leaves SAFE active, instruments off and sending off.
science.onboard-recovery.limitations: The incident is authored and seeded, not a calibrated single-event-upset probability inferred from ISS dose. The NASA avionics reference is archived and provides conceptual context, not current operational policy.
science.onboard-recovery.diagram: A reset leads to safe loads, cooldown and a powered recovery request before a deliberate operational restart.
science.capture-reserve.title: Capture demand and planning reserve
science.capture-reserve.summary: Technical Red Relay plans against a disclosed upper burn requirement, not only the nominal capture demand.
science.capture-reserve.context: Compare nominal demand, the upper planning envelope, loaded capability and reserve. Tank mass and propellant cost remain part of the same spacecraft design.
science.capture-reserve.consequence: A single seeded realization chooses actual burn demand inside the envelope. Confirmation consumes computed propellant; insufficient capability fails with the planning and realized quantities recorded.
science.capture-reserve.deeper: The rocket equation relates mass ratio, specific impulse and achievable velocity change. Reserve must be loaded before launch and cannot be granted at arrival.
science.capture-reserve.limitations: Uncertainty affects burn demand, not a propagated off-nominal orbit or navigation solution. A successful capture uses the nominal teaching orbit; the envelope is an authored assumption.
science.capture-reserve.diagram: Nominal capture demand lies inside a bounded planning envelope; loaded propellant must cover the upper requirement.

science.orbital-speed.title: Why orbits need speed, not just height
science.orbital-speed.summary: An orbit is falling forward fast enough that the ground curves away as quickly as you fall.
science.orbital-speed.context: At 200 km the circular speed is 7.78 km/s and one lap takes about 88.5 minutes; at 800 km it is 7.45 km/s.
science.orbital-speed.consequence: Reaching 200 km straight up costs little; staying there needs about 7.8 km/s of sideways speed, which is why rockets spend most of their fuel going sideways.
science.orbital-speed.deeper: Circular speed is v = sqrt(mu / r). Lower orbits are faster and shorter; raising an orbit makes the craft slower, even though the burn speeded it up.
science.orbital-speed.limitations: Gravity is a single point mass; Earth’s bulge, drag at orbital height and other pulls are not modelled, so these orbits never decay.
science.orbital-speed.diagram: A cannonball fired faster and faster from a mountain: it lands, lands farther, then keeps missing the ground.
science.gravity-turn.title: The gravity turn: rise, tip over, let gravity bend the path
science.gravity-turn.summary: The rocket climbs straight up through the thick air, tips slightly, then follows its own velocity so gravity bends the path toward horizontal.
science.gravity-turn.context: Your ascent settings are the vertical rise time, the size and length of the pitch kick, the launch azimuth and the stage-1 fuel load.
science.gravity-turn.consequence: A kick that is too small leaves you high and slow and falling back; too large and you turn over while still low, burn through thick air sideways and may hit the ground.
science.gravity-turn.deeper: During the turn thrust points along the air-relative velocity, so there is almost no steering loss. Azimuth 90 degrees (due east) from 28.5 degrees north gives a 28.5 degree orbit and borrows about 0.4 km/s from Earth’s spin.
science.gravity-turn.limitations: The pitch profile is a simple ramp, not an optimised trajectory. There are no winds, no weather and no structural limits beyond the stated dynamic-pressure readout.
science.gravity-turn.diagram: A path that starts vertical and gradually bends over until it is moving along the horizon at the target height.
science.gravity-drag-losses.title: Why orbit costs about 9.4 km/s, not 7.8
science.gravity-drag-losses.summary: Gravity pulls back while you climb and air drags you; both waste some of the rocket’s velocity change.
science.gravity-drag-losses.context: The ascent preview reports the gravity, drag and steering losses separately so you can see where the budget went.
science.gravity-drag-losses.consequence: Climbing slowly or lingering in thick air raises losses; thrusting hard and tipping over early lowers gravity loss but can raise drag and steering loss.
science.gravity-drag-losses.deeper: Delta-v spent equals orbital speed plus gravity loss (about g times burn time spent climbing), drag loss and steering loss, minus Earth’s rotation bonus.
science.gravity-drag-losses.limitations: Losses come from a simple exponential atmosphere cut off at 150 km and a constant-g approximation inside each step.
science.gravity-drag-losses.diagram: A bar split into useful speed, gravity loss, drag loss and steering loss.
science.dynamic-pressure.title: Dynamic pressure: the squeeze of fast air
science.dynamic-pressure.summary: Dynamic pressure is half the air density times speed squared; it peaks where the rocket is already fast but the air is still thick.
science.dynamic-pressure.context: The ascent readout shows the pressure and marks its peak (max-q) as an event.
science.dynamic-pressure.consequence: Real rockets throttle or limit pitching near max-q; here it is a readout that shows why the early climb should not be rushed.
science.dynamic-pressure.deeper: q = 0.5 rho v^2, with density falling about 63 percent every 7.2 km.
science.dynamic-pressure.limitations: No structural failure is modelled; the number teaches, it does not break the vehicle.
science.dynamic-pressure.diagram: A curve that rises, peaks about a minute into flight, then falls as the air thins.
science.staging.title: Staging: throw away the empty tank
science.staging.summary: Dropping empty structure means the remaining fuel pushes a lighter rocket.
science.staging.context: Each launcher lists stage masses, thrust and efficiency; separation happens when a stage runs dry.
science.staging.consequence: More stages help until the extra structure and complexity outweigh the gain; the payload limit shows what each vehicle can lift.
science.staging.deeper: The rocket equation applies to each stage: delta-v = Isp x g0 x ln(m_start / m_end). Two stages beat one because the second ignores the first stage’s dry mass.
science.staging.limitations: Stages separate instantly with no tip-off or recontact, and fairing mass is a fixed number.
science.staging.diagram: Two stacked stacks of boxes; the lower one falls away when empty.
science.vis-viva.title: Vis-viva: speed at any point of an orbit
science.vis-viva.summary: One equation links your speed, your distance and the size of your orbit.
science.vis-viva.context: The orbit panel and the burn planner use it to turn a target orbit into a required speed.
science.vis-viva.consequence: Faster than circular speed at a point lifts the opposite side of the orbit; slower lowers it.
science.vis-viva.deeper: v^2 = mu (2 / r - 1 / a). With v = sqrt(2 mu / r) the energy is zero and the path is a parabola; faster is a hyperbola.
science.vis-viva.limitations: Point-mass gravity only, so the result is exact in the model but not a real navigation solution.
science.vis-viva.diagram: An ellipse with speeds marked at the lowest and highest point.
science.burn-direction.title: Which way to burn
science.burn-direction.summary: A burn along your motion raises the opposite side of the orbit; against your motion lowers it; sideways turns the orbit plane.
science.burn-direction.context: Burns are set by size and direction relative to your motion (along, sideways, outward) and by when they fire.
science.burn-direction.consequence: Prograde at periapsis raises the apoapsis; retrograde at apoapsis lowers the periapsis; normal burns change inclination at a high price.
science.burn-direction.deeper: The planner uses the along-track, orbit-normal and outward directions of your current state; a burn changes velocity instantly and costs propellant by the rocket equation.
science.burn-direction.limitations: Burns are instantaneous, with no finite burn time, gravity loss or pointing error.
science.burn-direction.diagram: Arrows along, across and outward from a spacecraft on an ellipse.
science.hohmann-transfer.title: Two burns to change orbit
science.hohmann-transfer.summary: To reach a higher circular orbit, burn once to stretch the orbit out to the new height, then burn again at the top to make it round.
science.hohmann-transfer.context: Raise Your Orbit uses exactly this: a first burn at your current height and a second burn one half-orbit later.
science.hohmann-transfer.consequence: The two burns together cost the least fuel for a circle-to-circle change; waiting between them costs time, not fuel.
science.hohmann-transfer.deeper: From 200 km to geostationary needs 2.45 km/s then 1.48 km/s. The transfer lasts half the transfer ellipse’s period.
science.hohmann-transfer.limitations: Real burns take time and aim errors need corrections; both are outside this model.
science.hohmann-transfer.diagram: Two circles joined by a half-ellipse with a burn marked at each end.
science.escape-velocity.title: Escape: enough energy to never come back
science.escape-velocity.summary: At escape speed the orbit is no longer closed; any more and the craft leaves with speed to spare.
science.escape-velocity.context: Past Earth asks you to leave with speed above a stated margin, measured from your actual state.
science.escape-velocity.consequence: From 200 km, 11.0 km/s is escape speed, only 3.2 km/s above circular; excess speed beyond that is what travels with you in deep space.
science.escape-velocity.deeper: Escape speed is sqrt(2) times circular speed; excess speed v_inf satisfies v_inf^2 = v^2 - 2 mu / r.
science.escape-velocity.limitations: Earth’s own pull on the departing craft is exact in the model; the Sun’s pull is not included here.
science.escape-velocity.diagram: A dashed parabola with a hyperbola just outside it.
science.deorbit-entry.title: Leaving orbit: lower the low point
science.deorbit-entry.summary: A retrograde burn drops the low point of the orbit into the atmosphere, where the craft would be slowed down and brought home.
science.deorbit-entry.context: Leave Orbit Safely is complete when the path crosses the 100 km entry height.
science.deorbit-entry.consequence: A small burn at the high point lowers the low point a lot; burning at the wrong place wastes fuel.
science.deorbit-entry.deeper: The burn at apoapsis lowers periapsis to R + 70 km or lower; speed lost is the difference between circular and transfer speeds at that radius.
science.deorbit-entry.limitations: There is no re-entry heating or guidance model: crossing the entry height is the stated finish.
science.deorbit-entry.diagram: An orbit with its low point dipping through a thin shaded atmosphere ring.
science.sphere-of-influence.title: Where the Moon takes over: the sphere of influence
science.sphere-of-influence.summary: Near the Moon its gravity matters more than Earth’s, so the model switches the controlling body at a boundary.
science.sphere-of-influence.context: The Moon’s boundary is 66,170 km in this model; the switch keeps position and velocity continuous.
science.sphere-of-influence.consequence: Inside it, orbit numbers are measured around the Moon; outside, around Earth. The same spacecraft is simply described from another point of view.
science.sphere-of-influence.deeper: Patched conics: each stretch is a two-body conic; at the boundary the Moon-relative state equals the Earth-relative state minus the Moon’s own position and velocity.
science.sphere-of-influence.limitations: The real boundary is not a sharp sphere, and Sun and Earth pulls inside it are ignored.
science.sphere-of-influence.diagram: A small circle around the Moon on the Earth–Moon line.
science.trans-lunar-injection.title: Trans-lunar injection: the big push toward the Moon
science.trans-lunar-injection.summary: One burn near the low point of a parking orbit stretches the path out until it touches the Moon’s distance days later.
science.trans-lunar-injection.context: From a 200 km parking orbit the burn adds about 3.13 km/s; the trip to 384,400 km takes about five days.
science.trans-lunar-injection.consequenc: Too little and you fall short; too much and you arrive early or miss; the right size and moment make the Moon meet you.
science.trans-lunar-injection.deeper: The transfer is an ellipse with apoapsis at the Moon’s distance; the burn is best near periapsis because speed is highest there.
science.trans-lunar-injection.limitation: The Moon is on a fixed circular path and is not pulled by the spacecraft.
science.trans-lunar-injection.diagram: Parking circle, long ellipse to the Moon’s orbit and the Moon at its arrival position.
science.lunar-phasing.title: Phasing: aiming where the Moon will be
science.lunar-phasing.summary: The Moon moves about 0.55 degrees every hour, so the burn must be timed and aimed for where it will be days later.
science.lunar-phasing.context: Parking-orbit plane and burn moment are searched against the Moon’s real position in the model.
science.lunar-phasing.consequence: A burn a few minutes late shifts the arrival by thousands of kilometres; a wrong plane means the Moon is off to the side.
science.lunar-phasing.deeper: The Moon’s orbit is inclined to Earth’s equator; a launch window is when your orbit plane contains the Moon’s future position.
science.lunar-phasing.limitations: The Moon follows a fixed circular path with a fixed node, not the real ephemeris.
science.lunar-phasing.diagram: A parking ring with the burn point opposite the Moon’s arrival point.
science.lunar-capture.title: Capture: slow down at the Moon or fly on by
science.lunar-capture.summary: Arriving fast, the craft swings past the Moon and leaves unless a burn at the closest point slows it into orbit.
science.lunar-capture.context: Earth to the Moon burns against the direction of travel at the lunar periapsis; the amount sets the new orbit’s size.
science.lunar-capture.consequence: About 0.82 km/s turns a 100 km flyby into a 100 km circular orbit; a smaller burn leaves a long loop.
science.lunar-capture.deeper: Arrival speed at the boundary (excess speed about 0.83 km/s) plus the Moon’s pull gives hyperbolic speed at periapsis; captured speed is below the Moon’s escape speed there.
science.lunar-capture.limitations: No gravity from Earth or Sun is applied inside the Moon’s region, and burns are instantaneous.
science.lunar-capture.diagram: A hyperbola bending around the Moon and an ellipse after the retrograde burn.
science.trajectory-model-limits.title: What this trajectory model leaves out
science.trajectory-model-limits.summary: The model is honest about its simplifications: they are shown in the interface and in every export.
science.trajectory-model-limits.context: Point-mass gravity, instant burns, a Moon on rails, two-body regions patched at a boundary, a simple atmosphere during ascent and no re-entry.
science.trajectory-model-limits.conseque: Results are right for the model and good for learning, not for navigating a real spacecraft.
science.trajectory-model-limits.deeper: Where a real tool would integrate many forces, this one switches between exact two-body solutions; the checks against NASA’s GMAT reproduce two-body motion to well under a metre.
science.trajectory-model-limits.limitati: Anything not listed above — solar radiation pressure, J2, third-body perturbations, finite burns, re-entry — is not modelled.
science.trajectory-model-limits.diagram: A list of simplifications beside the trajectory.
